title: Nanook of the North
byline: Dir. Robert J. Flaherty; prod. Revillon Frères; dist. Pathé Exchange (US, 1922)

evidence.note: Published in the United States on 11 June 1922 via Pathé Exchange. The pre-1923 bright line applies regardless of any renewal question: every US work published before 1923 is public domain today by term expiry, full stop, under any version of the maximum term the 1909 Act and its extensions ever allowed. This is the operative basis for the verdict below and does not depend on whether a renewal was ever filed.
evidence.source: US Copyright Office Circular 15a: Duration of Copyright (authority on pre-1978 term limits)

evidence.note: Whether a renewal was ever filed is NOT settled, and a flat 'no renewal was filed' claim is not supportable: a full-text search of the Catalog of Copyright Entries, Cumulative Series, Motion Pictures 1940-1949 (archive.org) turns up an entry reading 'NANOOK OF THE NORTH. Revillon Freres, c1922...' with a separate claimant-index line '*Nanook of the North, 1922, REYNOLDS, E. A.' This could be evidence of a later renewal or re-registration under claimant Reynolds, E.A., or could be an unrelated catalog cross-reference — the OCR and format do not resolve it either way. Because the pre-1923 bright line above already settles the print's status, this question does not need to be answered to reach the verdict.
evidence.source: Catalog of Copyright Entries, Cumulative Series, Motion Pictures 1940-1949 (archive.org)

evidence.note: Nanook of the North is a silent film; the 1922 print contains no recorded musical track and no sound copyright exists in the original work. The visual content is freely usable. However, virtually every commercially distributed copy since the 1970s carries a separately composed and copyrighted musical accompaniment. Stanley Silverman composed a 1973 orchestral score for Films Inc./McGraw-Hill's educational release (LCCN 77701529, 1977 reissue). Gabriel Thibaudeau composed a new score for the 2014 Flicker Alley/Lobster Films Blu-ray restoration. Any copy of the film that includes one of these—or any other post-1922—score carries a separate, active copyright in that musical recording. A creator editing the mute 1922 picture may add their own music freely; lifting an existing accompaniment without clearance infringes that score's copyright independently of the film's public-domain status.
evidence.source: Archive.org item nanookofthenorthreel2 metadata: Films Inc./McGraw-Hill version with 1973 Stanley Silverman score (LCCN 77701529, uploaded by associate-yvonne-wang@archive.org)

evidence.note: Nanook of the North is an original observational documentary; Flaherty filmed actual Inuit life in the Ungava Peninsula region of northern Quebec (with staged elements) and did not adapt a pre-existing protected literary work. Flaherty's companion book 'My Eskimo Friends' (Doubleday, 1924) post-dates the film by two years and was not its narrative source. The editorial structure and content originate in the 1922 film itself, so the story shares the film's 1922 US publication date and is free by the same pre-1923 bright line as the print, regardless of whether a renewal was ever filed.
evidence.source: US Copyright Office Circular 15a: Duration of Copyright

evidence.note: A faithful restoration of a public-domain film adds no new US copyright: copying or restoring public-domain images without original creative additions is not protected (Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp., S.D.N.Y. 1999, following Feist v. Rural, 1991). What a restoration ADDS can be protected: a newly composed or newly recorded score, colorization, newly written or translated titles and subtitles, and other original additions. Separately, ripping a copy-protected Blu-ray or DVD can break the DMCA's anti-circumvention rule (17 U.S.C. 1201) even when the film itself is public domain.
evidence.source: Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp. (summary)

evidence.note: 17 U.S.C. 1201 - circumvention of copyright protection systems.

At least two commercially distributed modern restorations are in active circulation. (1) Flicker Alley / Lobster Films, 2014 Blu-ray: restored from the original nitrate negative held by Fondation Pathé (Paris), credited to Lobster Films, Groupama Gan Foundation for Cinema, and Fondation Pathé; includes a new orchestral score by Gabriel Thibaudeau; distributed in the US by Flicker Alley. The restored image-work and the commissioned score each carry independent copyright. (2) Criterion Collection Eclipse Series 33: Early Flaherty (Spine 33, 2011). Copying from either commercial release without authorisation infringes those restoration copyrights even though the underlying 1922 print is public domain. Users seeking only PD material should use a silent, non-restoration source such as archive.org/details/NanookOfTheNorth and verify the file carries no copyrighted accompaniment.
evidence.source: Flicker Alley Blu-ray (2014); Criterion Collection Eclipse Series 33: Early Flaherty (2011)

editorial:
Nanook of the North (1922) is Robert J. Flaherty's landmark observational documentary following Allakariallak and his family surviving in the Ungava Peninsula of northern Quebec. Financed by the French fur-trading firm Revillon Frères and distributed in the United States by Pathé Exchange—premiering theatrically on 11 June 1922—it became one of the first feature-length nonfiction films to achieve wide commercial release. The original print is public domain in the US on the simplest possible basis: every US work published before 1923 is free today by term expiry, regardless of renewal history. Whether a renewal was ever filed is not actually settled — a primary-source search turned up an ambiguous entry that may or may not be one — but it does not need to be, because the pre-1923 cutoff already covers it. The visual content of the 1922 film has circulated without license ever since and may be freely recut, excerpted, or redistributed.

The practical rights trap is the score. Because this is a silent film, the original 1922 print contains no music—but virtually every commercially distributed copy carries a separately composed and copyrighted accompaniment. Stanley Silverman's 1973 orchestral arrangement appears on the Films Inc. educational version; Gabriel Thibaudeau's score accompanies the 2014 Flicker Alley Blu-ray, which was also restored from Fondation Pathé's original nitrate negative; a faithful restoration of public-domain images does not create a new US copyright in those images, but the score remains independently protected. A creator using footage from Archive.org should confirm the file is a mute or intertitle-only copy to avoid a copyrighted accompanying score; ripping from the Flicker Alley or Criterion Eclipse discs instead could violate DMCA anti-circumvention rules even though the underlying images are public domain.
faq: Can I upload or monetize Nanook of the North footage on YouTube or Vimeo?

The underlying 1922 picture is public domain in the US and you do not need permission to use it. The practical danger is the audio track. If your copy includes a musical score—Stanley Silverman's 1973 arrangement, Gabriel Thibaudeau's 2014 Flicker Alley score, or any other post-1922 accompaniment—that audio is separately copyrighted and can trigger a Content ID claim or takedown even though the film's images are free. Use a silent version or add your own music to avoid this problem. Also avoid ripping directly from the Flicker Alley Blu-ray or Criterion Eclipse disc; those are copy-protected, and circumventing that protection can violate DMCA anti-circumvention rules even though the underlying images are public domain.
Does Revillon Frères or any estate still own rights to the original 1922 film?

No. The US print is public domain under the pre-1923 bright line regardless of renewal history, so no entity—including Revillon Frères, Pathé Exchange, or Flaherty's estate—holds a US copyright in it today. Whether a renewal was ever filed in the 1940s-50s is not fully settled from the record checked, but it does not matter: the pre-1923 cutoff covers the print either way. What does survive are the copyrights in separately composed scores and other original additions attached to distributed copies; a faithful image restoration of a public-domain film does not create a new US copyright in those images. The bare 1922 footage is unowned from a US copyright standpoint.
